ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure, the power supply E and internal resistance r are connected in series in the same branch; at the upper right there is resistor R1, and at the middle-lower right there is resistor R2, with R1 and R2 connected at the middle node; voltmeter V is connected between this middle node and the lower common node; on the right side there is also resistor R3, whose upper end is connected to the middle node through switch S, and whose lower end is connected to the lower common node. Therefore, when S is closed, R3 and R2 are connected between the same pair of nodes, forming a parallel connection, and what the voltmeter measures is the voltage across the R2, R3 parallel branch. Reasoning: Treat the voltmeter as an ideal voltmeter, so it does not affect the circuit. After S is closed, R2 = 4Ω and R3 = 4Ω are in parallel, so R23 = 4Ω || 4Ω = 2Ω. In the whole loop, the power supply internal resistance r, R1, and the parallel equivalent resistance R23 are in series, so the total resistance Rtotal = r + R1 + R23 = 1Ω + 1Ω + 2Ω = 4Ω. The loop current I = E / Rtotal = 12V / 4Ω = 3A. The voltmeter is connected across the two ends of the parallel branch, so its reading U = I × R23 = 3A × 2Ω = 6V.

method.method_draft: Let the bottom rail be 0 V and let the voltage at the junction of R1, R2, voltmeter, and closed-switch path to R3 be V; this V is the voltmeter reading. Because R2 and R3 both go from this node to the bottom rail, the load current leaving the node is V/4 + V/4 = V/2.
